Stated Claim / Post Context:
First Global Girls’ Index finds health gains in 178 countries

Actual Article Body:
Belinda Roozemond | Posted on October 14, 2026 |

Health outcomes for girls improved in 178 of 192 countries between 2000 and 2023, according to the first Global Girls’ Index. Mortality among girls more than halved and birth rates among girls aged 10 to 19 fell by around one-third, although 290 million girls still live in countries with low or very low scores.

Health outcomes for girls improved in 178 of the 192 countries examined between 2000 and 2023, according to the first-ever Weltmädchenindex, or Global Girls’ Index.

Developed jointly by Plan International Germany and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV) at Ruhr University Bochum, the index compares health outcomes for just over 971 million girls and young women aged 5 to 19.

While the findings show substantial progress, major inequalities remain. Around 290 million girls still live in countries that score low or very low on the index.

“The findings show that funding makes a difference, political commitment can drive change, and progress is possible,” said Petra Berner, CEO of Plan International Germany, at the launch of the index.

“The priority now is to protect the gains already made and reach the girls who have not yet benefited sufficiently from them. Their chances of living healthy lives on their own terms must not depend on where they were born.”

Researchers analysed data from 192 countries covering the period from 2000 to 2023. The first edition focuses on health and uses five indicators:

The data came from the United Nations World Population Prospects and the Global Burden of Disease study. Each indicator is converted into a score on a scale from zero to 100. The five scores are then combined into an overall index score, with higher scores indicating better health outcomes.

The index’s overall score points to clear, if uneven, progress. Between 2000 and 2023, the global average rose by 5.91 points, from 45.16 to 51.07 out of 100. Higher scores indicate better health outcomes.

One of the most significant changes was the decline in mortality among girls. The rate more than halved over the 23-year period, falling from nearly one death per 800 girls to approximately 1 per 1,700.

There was also a substantial fall in births among girls aged 10 to 19. In 2000, 1 in 31 girls in this age group gave birth. By 2023, the figure had fallen by around one-third, to 1 in 48.

The greatest regional improvements were recorded in sub-Saharan Africa, where the average score rose by 9.77 points, and South Asia, where it increased by 9.32 points.

At country level, Rwanda recorded the greatest improvement, with its score rising by 33.07 points. It was followed by Ethiopia, with an increase of 29.78 points, and Burundi, with 27.52 points.

According to the report, one of the most important advances was the decline in mortality among girls, which more than halved between 2000 and 2023.

Among girls aged 10 to 19, the likelihood of giving birth also fell by around one-third over the same period.

Progress on maternal mortality and sexually transmitted diseases was far more limited. Between 2000 and 2023, the corresponding index scores rose by only 0.72 and 1.04 points respectively.

According to UN inter-agency estimates, the global lifetime risk of dying from a maternal cause for a 15-year-old girl was 1 in 272 in 2023, equivalent to approximately 0.37%. The index found that more than half of maternal deaths among girls and young women occurred in countries in its lowest category.

Despite the overall improvement, the Global Girls’ Index reveals substantial regional inequalities. In 2023, sub-Saharan Africa had an average score of 30.83 points. By comparison, Europe scored 71.64, East Asia 65.26 and North America 64.25. The regions making the fastest progress also started from some of the lowest scores. Despite these gains, the gap between regions remains wide.

The authors also highlight limitations in the available data. Detailed information is often unavailable on mental health, vaccination rates, access to healthcare and girls’ ability to make decisions about their own sexual and reproductive health.

A more comprehensive Global Girls’ Index is due to be published in 2028. According to Plan International Germany and the IFHV, it will also cover education, safety, equal opportunities and inclusion.
